drills.q: Given a sorted array and a target sum, what's the two-pointer move rule and why is it always safe?
drills.a: If current sum < target, move left right (only increasing the sum can help); if sum > target, move right left (only decreasing can help). Safe because sortedness guarantees the move you don't take can never produce the missed pair without also being reachable by the move you did take.

drills.q: Why is left < right the correct loop guard for pair-finding two pointers, not left <= right?
drills.a: left <= right permits left == right, letting a single element be used as both halves of the pair, producing a false positive match.

drills.q: Walk through why moving the shorter wall in Container With Most Water is provably correct.
drills.a: Area is bounded by min(height[left], height[right]) * width. If you move the taller pointer, the bound is still set by the shorter wall (now possibly at a smaller width), so area can't improve. Only moving the shorter pointer has a chance to raise the bounding height, so it's the only move that can find a better answer.

drills.q: In 3Sum, why must you skip duplicate values AFTER a match rather than skip duplicates unconditionally before checking sums?
drills.a: Skipping unconditionally before checking could skip over the actual valid current match. Duplicates must be identified as duplicates only once a valid triplet is found and recorded, then both left and right are advanced past any repeats of the values just used.

drills.q: Derive the O(1) extra space version of Trapping Rain Water from the O(n) space version that precomputes left_max[] and right_max[] arrays.
drills.a: Instead of precomputing both arrays fully, converge two pointers from the ends while tracking one running left_max and one running right_max scalar. At each step, advance the pointer on the side with the smaller running max, since that max is the true bound at that position, and add (max - height[pointer]) to the total before advancing.

drills.q: A candidate solves 4Sum with four independent nested loops (no two-pointer inner scan). What's the complexity cost of that choice, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Four naive nested loops is O(n^4). The fix: fix the outermost two indices with nested loops (each skipping duplicates), then run the two-pointer scan on the remaining sorted suffix for the last two indices, giving O(n^3) -- one full loop level cheaper.

drills.q: Design a solution for finding the pair of numbers in a sorted array whose sum is CLOSEST to a target (not necessarily equal). How does the pointer movement rule change from exact Two Sum?
drills.a: Same converging pointers and same move rule (sum < target -> left++, sum > target -> right--), but instead of returning immediately on equality, track a running best = min(abs(sum-target)) across the entire walk and update it every iteration; only exit early if sum == target exactly, since nothing can beat an exact match.

drills.q: A candidate claims two pointers can be applied directly to an unsorted array as long as you track the original indices in parallel. Is this correct?
drills.a: No -- the correctness proof for converging two pointers depends on sortedness (or another monotonic property) to guarantee that advancing one specific pointer can't skip the answer. Tracking original indices alongside an unsorted array doesn't restore that monotonic guarantee; you'd need to actually sort (losing O(1) extra bookkeeping unless you sort index-value pairs) or fall back to a hash map.
